title: Cut the charge for downtown parking
summary: Lowers or scraps the daily charge in Town-run parking downtown, where on-street parking is $2.00 an hour and most lots are $1.50.

how: Staff bring the parking fee schedule to Town Council with the budget.
Residents and downtown businesses comment at the budget public hearing.
Town Council adopts the fee schedule.

params.label: Change in the daily parking charge

evidence.claim: Chapel Hill charges $2.00 an hour on street from 8am to 6pm Monday to Saturday, and about $1.50 an hour in most Town lots
evidence.source: Town of Chapel Hill, Parking Fee Schedule

evidence.claim: The Town's Parking Facilities Fund is $6,468,125 in 2026-27, of which about $4.2 million is debt on the 125 East Rosemary deck — already helped by a $1.96 million transfer from the Town's debt fund
evidence.source: Town of Chapel Hill, 2026-27 Adopted Budget, Parking Facilities Fund, pp. 245-249

evidence.claim: Pricing curb spaces so a few stay open cut the miles driven circling for parking, and the emissions from them, by 30% against control blocks in San Francisco's SFpark pilot — a test of demand pricing against flat pricing, not against free
evidence.source: San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency, SFpark evaluation (2014) — the agency's own evaluation of its pilot

evidence.claim: Across 22 studies in 15 cities, cars hunting for underpriced curb parking made up between 8% and 74% of traffic — a wide range, and the authors warn researchers tend to count cruising only where they expect to find it
evidence.source: Hampshire & Shoup, How Much Traffic is Cruising for Parking?, Transfers Magazine no. 4 (2019)

evidence.claim: Old Pasadena metered its curb in 1993 and spent the money on its own sidewalks, alleys and services; by 2001 its 690 meters netted $1.2 million a year and its sales tax takings had overtaken the nearby mall that parked people free
evidence.source: Kolozsvari & Shoup, Turning Small Change into Big Changes, ACCESS no. 23 (2003) — a case study, with no control group

evidence.claim: North Carolina requires that money from on-street parking meters be spent enforcing and administering traffic and parking rules, so going free also defunds the enforcement of time limits, disabled bays and fire lanes

pros: Downtown competes with suburban centres that park people free, and the charge plus the risk of a ticket is the complaint Franklin Street merchants hear most.
Cheaper parking is an immediate, visible cut in the cost of coming downtown — the fastest thing a council can do that shoppers notice.
cons: The deck debt still has to be paid, so around $4 million of parking fees has to come off the property tax instead — charging every household for spaces used mostly by people who drive in.
Spaces priced at nothing stay full, so drivers circle for one. How much traffic that adds is genuinely uncertain, but the pricing experiments all run the other way.
The retail case is the weakest part of it: Old Pasadena out-earned a free-parking mall by charging for the curb and spending the money on the street.
